Elemental analysis. The analysis of petroleum to determine the percentages of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, and sulfur (C, H, N, O, and S) is perhaps the first method used to examine the general nature and perform an evaluation of a feedstock and hydrocracked products. The analyses are carried out in an elemental analyser (e.g., CHN‐2000 from LECO) according to ASTM D‐5185 methods. The atomic ratios of the various ­elements to carbon (i.e. H/C, N/C, O/C, and S/C) are frequently used as indicators of the overall character of the feedstock and products. It is also of value to determine the amounts of trace elements, such as vanadium and nickel, in a feedstock since these materials can have serious deleterious effects on catalyst performance during refining by catalytic processes (Speight 2007). The ASTM methods for ultimate elemental analysis of petroleum products are illustrated in Figure 1.3. Metal content. A variety of tests (ASTM D‐1026, ASTM D‐1262, ASTM D‐1318, ASTM D‐1368, ASTM D‐1548, ASTM D‐1549, ASTM D‐2547, ASTM D‐2599, ASTM D‐2788, ASTM D‐3340, ASTM D‐3341, and ASTM D‐3605) have been designated for the determination of metals in petroleum products. Determination of metals in whole feeds can be accomplished by combustion of the sample so that only inorganic ash remains. The ash can then be digested with acid and the solution is examined for metal species by atomic absorption (AA) spectroscopy or inductively coupled argon plasma (ICAP) spectrometry (Speight 2007).

The methodology for metal determination includes sample preparation, sample digestion, and metal quantification. The size and type of reactor have little effect on performance, but it is vital for the experimental reactor to resemble as closely as possible one of the ideal reactors shown in Figure 2.4. The choice of reactor is mainly based on whether it can operate in isothermal conditions (good for obtaining kinetic parameters) or non‐isothermal mode, which provides relatively more complex results. A detailed account of the various types of reactors and their operations modes is given by Ancheyta (2017). The main role of a laboratory reactor is to derive the kinetic equation using various reaction parameters such as pressure, temperature, ­contact time (liquid hourly space‐velocity, LHSV), hydrogen‐to‐oil ratio, etc. The purpose of this chapter is to examine a laboratory micro‐testing reactor that can be used for the hydroprocessing (hydrotreating and hydrocracking) reaction and determine the role of support and catalyst in catalytic activities. The reaction is carried out at atmospheric pressure using a plug‐flow glass reactor system. Based on the reaction to be studied, the limiting reactant can vary as a model feed to test the catalyst, e.g. isopropanol (IPA), cumene, cyclohexene, furan, and thiophene. However, the quality of results obtained from these experiments depends on the procedure applied for calibration or standardization of the testing equipment. Some limitations associated with the plug‐flow reactor system are listed in Table 2.1.
2.2 ­Glass Microreactor Design and Experimentation A microreactor uses a small amount of catalyst that typically ranges between 10 and 500 mg. It commonly uses a glass reactor, which means there is a low‐pressure reaction, usually at atmospheric pressure. The notion of small volume systems is several decades old and has given rise to a significant number of publications as well as considerable interest among the research community (Rouhi 2004). However, the design specifications and operational considerations of a microreactor system have also been used by other research scientists who have constructed different units for their requirements. The designed system allows the researcher to make a quick evaluation of a catalyst prototype, particularly at the primary stage of a new project. The catalytic activity data can be utilized for reaction ­kinetics and comparison between catalysts as well as in catalyst stability over time

Since oxygen chemisorption cannot distinguish the different sites generated by the promoters or by the interaction of the active metal with the promoters or the sulfur species, a more advanced technique may be required to estimate the promoted sites using spectroscopic techniques along with chemisorption. 3.1 ­Introduction Batch reactor tests can be envisaged as a second level of experimentation, after a preliminary evaluation of catalysts such as those in microflow glass reactors discussed in the previous chapter. The main differences between these types of reactors are listed in Table 3.1. As indicated by the name, batch reactors operate in a discontinuous mode, which means that the reactor is loaded with reagents and catalysts, then the desired test conditions are adjusted. Afterwards, the reaction is run for a previously decided period of time. Usually, samples are taken at regular time intervals and analyzed to monitor the reaction evolution. For hydrotreating catalysts the main reactions studied are hydrodesulfurization (HDS), hydrogenation (HYD), hydrocracking, hydrodenitrogenation (HDN), hydrodemetallation, and hydrodeoxygenation (HDO). Table 3.2 shows the common model molecules employed for every type of reaction. It is important to highlight that in some experiments the reactor feed may include several model molecules and even real feedstocks such as crude oils or petroleum distillates. Batch reactors are extensively employed for obtaining kinetic parameters of reactions with model compounds. The results are useful for screening and optimization of catalyst formulations and also for correlating catalyst properties, activity, and selectivity.

3.3.4  Analysis of the Reaction Samples Analysis of reaction products by gas chromatography deserves a brief explanation, given that obtaining reliable and reproducible results requires the development of an analytical method specially tailored to the particular reaction test. The procedure requires the selection of a separation column, and for flows and temperatures to be set in order to separate and quantify all the chemical compounds involved in the reactions. The most frequently used FID detector is non‐selective, which means that it responds to any hydrocarbon and does not distinguish one particular type of hydrocarbon from another. Moreover, when using an FID not all hydrocarbons yield the same response, which means that performing an adequate quantitative analysis requires calibration curves to be constructed for each chemical compound involved in the reaction. This is particularly critical when the aim of the research is to obtain kinetic parameters for complex reactions. Sometimes researchers face the challenge to establish a particular reaction network. In these cases, an analytical technique that can identify different chemical compounds must be used. A mass spectrometer (MS) is probably the best option for this type of study.

Nonetheless, experiments in batch reactors using model compounds allow the isolation of a particular reaction with the aim of obtaining a reliable measurement of catalytic activity, or in some cases the calculation of kinetic parameters. As well as carefully performing batch reaction experiments, obtaining reliable and reproducible results requires specialized characterization supported by analytical techniques in order to establish the complete reaction network and obtain a mass balance within an acceptable limit of deviation. These two elements are pivotal for the development of kinetic models useful in the scale‐up of reaction processes. The example developed in Section 3.3 shows that experimentation in a batch reactor with model compounds allow to information on catalytic phenomena to be obtained on several levels. The first and simplest level consists of measuring the conversion values of the model compound. The second level is the determination of apparent kinetic parameters, which encompasses several phenomena, such as global first‐order coefficients. The third level is the estimation of the kinetic parameters of all the reactions involved in the reaction ­network, and this is the level reached in the example developed in this chapter. A further level involves the determination of the various kinetic parameters involved in a complex reaction rate expression such as LHHW, provided that an adequate experiment design yields enough information to complete the task. To obtain true kinetic parameters, scientists must discard mass transfer effects. This can be done by two approaches: (i) by performing experiments changing stirring rate and particle size systematically to find the values at which the catalytic activity observed is no longer influenced by diffusion effects and (ii) by estimation of the effectiveness factor based on Thiele modulus calculus using data for reaction conditions and catalysts properties. In this approach the effectiveness factor must be very close to unity to ensure kinetic regime. With the advent of computational tools, solving equations and fitting systems data, including complex reaction networks and/or complex kinetic expressions, can be solved to determine all the kinetic parameters involved in hydrotreating reactions. Historically, batch reactor experiments have been used extensively in the scientific literature. Nonetheless, the potential for obtaining information about the kinetics of the catalytic reaction system in most cases has not been adequately exploited, since most catalytic activity results are reported at the level of conversion or apparent kinetics, and evidence of absence of diffusional control is seldom included. The next generation of researchers should take into account that data processing and kinetic modeling efforts may reveal interesting information concerning heterogeneous catalytic phenomena.

4.1 ­Introduction Laboratory studies generally have only an exploratory function when performing experiments for catalyst screening, evaluating the effect of some reaction conditions, generating data for kinetic studies, etc. Experiments in batch reactors are frequently used to develop kinetic models that will be used in the design of reactors. Prior to using kinetic models for the reactor design, the physical phenomena that occur within the reactor must be studied, such as diffusion limitation, which impacts on the conversion and selectivity of the products. The selection of a reactor for a given reaction can be done either by engineering methods or by a series analysis based on experimental studies. The proper definition of the type of reactor is an essential part in the design of a chemical reactor, as can be seen in Figure  4.1. It is clear from this figure that studies in a batch-scale reactor are important in order to obtain the intrinsic reaction rate and selectivity from which the kinetic equations can be derived. After having established the intrinsic reaction rate expressions, they are used to develop a large-scale mathematical model of the reactor. Experiments at pilot-plant scale can be omitted if the treatment of the physical processes of the model (velocity distribution, mixing, etc.) is adequate to predict their effects on conversion and selectivity, but this does not happen frequently, therefore one of the functions of the pilot plant is to evaluate and validate the reactor model. The pilot plant is also used to investigate possible problems of equipment construction materials, corrosion, instrumentation, operation, and control procedures, which are important in a large-scale unit.

3.1 ­Introduction Batch reactor tests can be envisaged as a second level of experimentation, after a preliminary evaluation of catalysts such as those in microflow glass reactors discussed in the previous chapter. The main differences between these types of reactors are listed in Table 3.1. As indicated by the name, batch reactors operate in a discontinuous mode, which means that the reactor is loaded with reagents and catalysts, then the desired test conditions are adjusted. Afterwards, the reaction is run for a previously decided period of time. Usually, samples are taken at regular time intervals and analyzed to monitor the reaction evolution. For hydrotreating catalysts the main reactions studied are hydrodesulfurization (HDS), hydrogenation (HYD), hydrocracking, hydrodenitrogenation (HDN), hydrodemetallation, and hydrodeoxygenation (HDO). Table 3.2 shows the common model molecules employed for every type of reaction. It is important to highlight that in some experiments the reactor feed may include several model molecules and even real feedstocks such as crude oils or petroleum distillates. Batch reactors are extensively employed for obtaining kinetic parameters of reactions with model compounds. The results are useful for screening and optimization of catalyst formulations and also for correlating catalyst properties, activity, and selectivity.

3.3.4  Analysis of the Reaction Samples Analysis of reaction products by gas chromatography deserves a brief explanation, given that obtaining reliable and reproducible results requires the development of an analytical method specially tailored to the particular reaction test. The procedure requires the selection of a separation column, and for flows and temperatures to be set in order to separate and quantify all the chemical compounds involved in the reactions. The most frequently used FID detector is non‐selective, which means that it responds to any hydrocarbon and does not distinguish one particular type of hydrocarbon from another. Moreover, when using an FID not all hydrocarbons yield the same response, which means that performing an adequate quantitative analysis requires calibration curves to be constructed for each chemical compound involved in the reaction. This is particularly critical when the aim of the research is to obtain kinetic parameters for complex reactions. Sometimes researchers face the challenge to establish a particular reaction network. In these cases, an analytical technique that can identify different chemical compounds must be used. A mass spectrometer (MS) is probably the best option for this type of study.

3.4.1  Reaction To study the HDS reaction of 4,6‐DMDBT a reaction mixture consisting of a solution of 4,6‐DMDBT in decane was used. The amount of 4,6‐DMDBT was adjusted to obtain a sulfur content of 0.1% by weight. In each experiment 40 mL of this solution was used. The reaction procedure is as follows. Nonetheless, experiments in batch reactors using model compounds allow the isolation of a particular reaction with the aim of obtaining a reliable measurement of catalytic activity, or in some cases the calculation of kinetic parameters. As well as carefully performing batch reaction experiments, obtaining reliable and reproducible results requires specialized characterization supported by analytical techniques in order to establish the complete reaction network and obtain a mass balance within an acceptable limit of deviation. These two elements are pivotal for the development of kinetic models useful in the scale‐up of reaction processes. The example developed in Section 3.3 shows that experimentation in a batch reactor with model compounds allow to information on catalytic phenomena to be obtained on several levels. The first and simplest level consists of measuring the conversion values of the model compound. The second level is the determination of apparent kinetic parameters, which encompasses several phenomena, such as global first‐order coefficients. The third level is the estimation of the kinetic parameters of all the reactions involved in the reaction ­network, and this is the level reached in the example developed in this chapter. A further level involves the determination of the various kinetic parameters involved in a complex reaction rate expression such as LHHW, provided that an adequate experiment design yields enough information to complete the task. To obtain true kinetic parameters, scientists must discard mass transfer effects. This can be done by two approaches: (i) by performing experiments changing stirring rate and particle size systematically to find the values at which the catalytic activity observed is no longer influenced by diffusion effects and (ii) by estimation of the effectiveness factor based on Thiele modulus calculus using data for reaction conditions and catalysts properties. In this approach the effectiveness factor must be very close to unity to ensure kinetic regime. With the advent of computational tools, solving equations and fitting systems data, including complex reaction networks and/or complex kinetic expressions, can be solved to determine all the kinetic parameters involved in hydrotreating reactions. Historically, batch reactor experiments have been used extensively in the scientific literature. Nonetheless, the potential for obtaining information about the kinetics of the catalytic reaction system in most cases has not been adequately exploited, since most catalytic activity results are reported at the level of conversion or apparent kinetics, and evidence of absence of diffusional control is seldom included. The next generation of researchers should take into account that data processing and kinetic modeling efforts may reveal interesting information concerning heterogeneous catalytic phenomena.

4.1 ­Introduction Laboratory studies generally have only an exploratory function when performing experiments for catalyst screening, evaluating the effect of some reaction conditions, generating data for kinetic studies, etc. Experiments in batch reactors are frequently used to develop kinetic models that will be used in the design of reactors. Prior to using kinetic models for the reactor design, the physical phenomena that occur within the reactor must be studied, such as diffusion limitation, which impacts on the conversion and selectivity of the products. The selection of a reactor for a given reaction can be done either by engineering methods or by a series analysis based on experimental studies. The proper definition of the type of reactor is an essential part in the design of a chemical reactor, as can be seen in Figure  4.1. It is clear from this figure that studies in a batch-scale reactor are important in order to obtain the intrinsic reaction rate and selectivity from which the kinetic equations can be derived. After having established the intrinsic reaction rate expressions, they are used to develop a large-scale mathematical model of the reactor. Experiments at pilot-plant scale can be omitted if the treatment of the physical processes of the model (velocity distribution, mixing, etc.) is adequate to predict their effects on conversion and selectivity, but this does not happen frequently, therefore one of the functions of the pilot plant is to evaluate and validate the reactor model. The pilot plant is also used to investigate possible problems of equipment construction materials, corrosion, instrumentation, operation, and control procedures, which are important in a large-scale unit.

In accordance with the NJDEP HDS Protocol, removal efficiency t esting was executed on the
First Defense ® HC 4-ft. unit in order to establish the ability of the FDHC to remove the specified

All results reported in this section were derived from test runs that fully complied with the terms
of the protocol. None of the collection intervals of the calibration samples excee ded one minute
in duration for any of the reported tests. The inlet feed concentration coefficient of variance
(COV) did not exceed 0.10 for any flow rate trials .

Built in 1808 in Philadelphia, the theatre was initially called The New Circus because instead of a proscenium stage and house, it had a hippodrome design with a central ring for animal acts. In 1811, the owners constructed an orchestra pit and proper stage for more traditional dramatic fare and the theatre was re-christened as The Olympic for its 1812 season. The first show was The Rivals by Richard Brinsley Sheridan. It would flip between being called The Olympic and Walnut Street Theatre until 1828. Edwin Booth would even become an owner of the theatre later in the century. The Walnut Street Theatre stands as a reminder of the longevity of theatricality in the United States. In honor of America’s #sesquicentennial, the company is currently running the musical 1776 by Stone & Edwards.

# Optimising energy use in an existing commercial building: a case study of Australia ’s Reef HQ Aquarium Sascha Thyer  & Severine Thomas &
Craig McClintock & Michael Ridd
> Received: 26 September 2016 / Accepted: 4 August 2017  
> #The Author(s) 2017. This article is an open access publication
Abstract Reef HQ Aquarium is a major tourism attrac-tion in tropical North Queensland, Australia. In 8 years, a 50% reduction in grid electricity was achieved through targeted infrastructure investment, whilst growing the business. Initially, grid energy consumption was 2438 MWh per annum, with 490-kW peak demand and energy intensity of 1625 MJ m −2 year −1 used on typical equipment such as HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning), machinery, lighting and catering equipment. Savings of 13% were achieved in the first year by increasing indoor air temperature set-points by 1.5 °C with no significant costs or impacts on occupant thermal comfort or worker productivity. Peak demand was decreased by 46% by upgrading the computerised building management system (BMS), HVAC, machin-ery and lighting; and by installing a 206-kW photovol-taic (PV) solar power system. This case study illustrates that (a) significant energy use reductions are possible at low cost; (b) capital investment in energy-efficient infra-structure can have short payback times and high direct and indirect benefits, particularly where equipment is ending its life. This study is unique as it examines how a com-mercial building with integrated chilled water thermal energy storage (TES) and a 3.2-ML chilled seawater aquarium system can be controlled by a BMS to optimise solar power to manage peak energy demand and also increase the utilisation of generated PV power in the absence of electrical battery storage. An interesting build-ing is used to demonstrate efficiency methods with ele-ments such as HVAC and lighting which usually consume over half commercial buildings ’ energy use.
